summary:
Caraga records no region-specific law or regulation bearing on trans people. A visitor there stands under the national framework of the Philippines, where same-sex conduct is legal and no provision of law criminalises a person for being transgender. The Caraga entry in the sourced reference material carries no separate finding on LGBT rights, so the national position governs in full.

Identity documents cannot be brought into line with a trans visitor's presentation. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A court order is the only route, so the marker a visitor carries at hotels, checkpoints and counters will remain the one assigned at birth.

No national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed repeatedly since 1999 without enactment, and protection runs only through local ordinances: eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities nationwide hold SOGIE anti-discrimination rules. Within Caraga, Butuan City, the regional capital and the most likely first port of call, adopted a non-discrimination ordinance in 2016, and Agusan del Norte and Dinagat Islands are among the covered provinces. Whether the remaining Caraga localities are covered is not resolved by the sourced material.

National recourses do exist for hostile speech. The Safe Spaces Act and the Magna Carta of Women reach slurs and ridicule with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar; the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers punishes SOGIE harassment with a fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty.

Shared facilities remain contested. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, alongside 22% support for same-sex civil unions. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised, the Family Code defining marriage as between a man and a woman.

Detention removes what protection exists on paper. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex; at Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and survival against abuse is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees to the City Jail Annex to prevent abuse.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent nationwide, though no incident in Caraga is recorded in the sourced material. Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a river in Cagayan on 23 June 2025; the same day a trans woman, a former journalist and activist, was shot inside a clinic in General Santos. A foreign national was arrested in May 2025 on a charge of raping a trans woman at a Batangas resort, and in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage in Bayambang, Pangasinan.

Entry and visa rules specific to trans visitors are not covered by the sourced material.
tangentialFactors:
A 2026 travel-risk assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers at 69 of 100 but scores trans travellers lower, at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band. Caraga itself is not scored.

Executive Order 100 s.2019, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 s.2023 added a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee. Neither had been implemented as of 2025, so the machinery a visitor might expect to reach does not function on the ground.

Campaigners attribute the absence of legislative remedy after two killings in June 2025 to the SOGIE Equality Bill's 25-year blockage in Congress. The Commission on Human Rights has described the trans killings recorded in a single year as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Social visibility is high and long-standing, with gender-diversity traditions carried under local names such as bakla and tomboy, prominent Pride events and nightlife, and substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. That visibility coexists with the lower trans-specific risk score and the documented 2025 killings.

A 2017 Human Rights Watch investigation recorded bullying and discrimination against gender-diverse students across Philippine schools while noting that law offered few remedies at the time. Schools are a further documented site of harm alongside streets and detention.
localsOnly:
The armed forces have permitted openly gay and bisexual personnel since 2009 and transgender personnel since 2017, with the uniform policy following the legal gender shown on the birth certificate. The Code of Professional Responsibility governing lawyers was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.

A pending bill would open legal gender recognition to applicants including consenting minors and would allow markers beyond male and female, such as X or nonbinary; its drafter links the absence of recognition to social exclusion, forced disclosure of trans status and violence. Allies have signalled endorsement of the bill to the 20th Congress. As of the sourced material it is not law.

Anti-discrimination ordinances operate at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels as well as city level, so residents in covered areas hold a local instrument with no national counterpart. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented arrangement at Davao City Jail houses three LGBT groupings in the City Jail Annex alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, transferred in batches to prevent abuse.

Local government and institutional posture varies within Caraga: Butuan City has held a non-discrimination ordinance since 2016, while the region's other localities are not enumerated in the sourced material.
outOfScopeNotes:
No region-specific enforcement finding or trans-related incident for Caraga is recorded in the sourced material; the Wikipedia entry for Caraga yields no usable finding on LGBT rights. The absence of a recorded incident is not evidence that none has occurred.

Which of Caraga's cities, municipalities and barangays hold non-discrimination ordinances beyond Butuan City is unresolved by the sources, as is enforcement practice under the ordinances that do exist.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans travellers arriving in the Philippines are not sourced here, and the sources do not address hotel, banking or airport document checks in Caraga.

Whether the Executive Order 100 and Executive Order 51 diversity machinery has any presence in Caraga is not sourced. Implementation is stated as absent nationally as of 2025.

The pending legal gender recognition bill's passage date, and the operation of court-petition routes for residents of Caraga, remain unresolved on this record.
